newsitem.title: UK: Ad group seeks data on pan-European TV market.
newsitem.headline: Ad group seeks data on pan-European TV market.

text.p: The European Association of Advertising Agencies (EAAA) said on Tuesday its Media Research Group is seeking ways to track data on the pan-European television market, in order to improve the sale of airtime to advertisers.

"There's more and more money going into international media, particularly international TV, because there are more and more international TV channels," Jane Perry, chairman of the Media Research Group for the EAAA, told Reuters in a telephone interview.

The Pan-European television market -- including both cable and satellite channels -- has exploded since CNN first entered the scene in the mid-1980s. But there remains a dearth of information about the size and nature of the television audience and the amount of advertising expenditure.
"We don't have any data on what the size of the market is," Perry said. "CNN probably has the highest audience, but we don't know."

While CNN and other pan-European channels -- such as the NBC Super Channel, BBC World, European Business, Euro News and Sky News -- collect data on their own audiences, they each collect data on different bases and issue figures at different times.

Perry, who is also European Media Research director for ad agency Young & Rubicam, said that despite the lack of solid data on the pan-European television market, selling airtime to advertisers had not been difficult. Advertisers were buying based on hunches and their own television viewing patterns.
"It's not hard to sell CNN to American advertisers," said Perry. "They watch it at home and they watch it when they travel overseas."
But better data would improve the market and remove much of the overlapping work now done by agencies trying to assess the market.
The EAAA said it was asking TV channels for household penetration data by country on a monthly basis.

The Register Group, a media research group, is also seeking data on the pan-European market. But Perry said Register was only measuring the number of ads broadcasat and using rate cards to determine total expenditure. Register plans to publish its data in 1998.

Perry said rate cards provided a poor way of measuring advertising expenditure because international television airtime was heavily discounted. In addition, most channels derived more money from sponsorship deals than from advertising, she said.
